notes:
I couldn't find sources for every verse, so coverage is uneven. Several full pages (Enduring Word, bible.org/Utley) were cut off before verse 30, so for those I only had short search excerpts. Where I found nothing on a verse or a tradition, I've said so.

## Part 1: What each verse means (traditional reading)

**v. 29:** Utley's notes on bible.org say John was clearly within God's will, even though his ministry lasted only about eighteen months. Wicked scheming caused his death, but God still controls history. (https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-6)
- Matthew Henry says those who fight God's cause are defeated even when they seem to win. He compares the witnesses who "rose again" in their successors (Rev. 11). (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_006.cfm)

**v. 30:** Precept Austin reminds readers what had just happened: John had been beheaded and buried, and the disciples had been ministering two by two. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary)

**v. 31:** Guzik says the disciples had just come back from a successful mission, and Jesus knew they needed rest. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/)
- A devotional quoted on Precept Austin makes the point that working until you are exhausted is not a virtue. By calling them away to rest first, Jesus showed He doesn't need our frantic effort to get His work done. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary)

**v. 33:** Precept Austin quotes the Expositor's commentary. It pictures each town adding its stream to a growing river of eager people, and calls this the peak of Jesus' popularity. John's Gospel shows it was also a turning point. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary)
- MacArthur (on the same page) calls the crowd's response "mixed and fickle." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary)

**v. 34:**
- **The disciples' view versus Jesus' view.** Guzik says the disciples often saw the crowds as work and demands. Jesus saw them with compassion. Sheep without a shepherd can't defend themselves against predators and struggle to find food and water. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/)
- **Bad shepherds.** Barnes, Poole and Gill point to the failed leaders of the day. Barnes says the priests and scribes were proud and corrupt and neglected ordinary people. Gill says Jesus put the public good ahead of His own wish for privacy. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-34.htm)
- **Old Testament background.** The Bible Hub study notes link the phrase to Numbers 27:17 (Moses asking for a leader) and Ezekiel 34 (God's charge against Israel's shepherds). They present Jesus as the Good Shepherd. (https://biblehub.com/study/mark/6-34.htm)
- **Chrysostom**, cited on Bible Hub, says the scribes were more like wolves than pastors. (https://biblehub.com/mark/6-34.htm)

**v. 37:**
- Matthew Henry notes that Jesus ordered that everyone be fed. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_006.cfm)
- Precept Austin cites John 6:6, where Jesus is said to be testing the disciples. The writer thinks the bigger aim was probably to get the disciples personally involved in caring for the crowd. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary)

**v. 38:** R.C. Sproul paraphrases Jesus as saying, in effect: bring what you have, let Me bless it, and see what God does. (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-feeding-five-thousand)

**v. 39–40:**
- Guzik says Jesus organized the crowd rather than letting it become a mob. He did this as their shepherd. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/)
- Spurgeon says Mark's Greek word pictures the groups like flower beds with paths between them. This let the servers reach everyone without confusion. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary)

**v. 41:**
- **Where the miracle happened.** Utley says the verbs (a one-time "broke," then an ongoing "kept giving") show the multiplying happened in Jesus' hands. Looking up to heaven showed His authority came from the Father. (https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-6) Guzik agrees the miracle seems to have happened in Jesus' hands. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/)
- **The blessing.** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) calls the blessing the turning point of the miracle. It says giving the bread through the disciples pointed ahead to them as His future ministers. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-41.html)
- Matthew Henry notes that Jesus said the blessing Himself, and the bread multiplied because of it. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_006.cfm)
- **Devotional readings.** F.E. Marsh says the broken bread pictures Christ's body broken in death. Handing bread to the disciples pictures the gospel entrusted to believers to pass on. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/marsh_fe/bible_readings/141.cfm)
- MacArthur says looking up to heaven acknowledges where all food comes from. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/41-30/the-creator-provides)

**v. 42:** Chuck Smith says the Greek word for "satisfied" really means stuffed: they ate until they couldn't eat any more. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-48.html)

**v. 43:**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the leftovers, far more than the food they started with, were striking proof that the miracle was real. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-41.html)
- Spurgeon notes there was a basketful for each of the twelve who served. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-52.html)
- Guzik's summary says the leftovers were gathered because waste doesn't honor the God who provides. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/)

**v. 44:**
- A NET Bible note (quoted on Precept Austin) says the Greek word means adult males. Matthew 14:21 adds women and children. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary)
- Some estimate 15,000–20,000 people in total. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary) MacArthur calls it really "a feeding of the twenty-five thousand." (https://www.gty.org/sermons/41-31/jesus-walks-on-water)
- MacArthur also sees it as a picture of God's common grace (His kindness to everyone, good and bad). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary)

**v. 45:**
- **Why the hurry.** Barclay thinks John 6 explains it: the crowd wanted to make Jesus king, and He had already rejected that path of power at His temptation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-50.html)
- **Which Bethsaida.** Hiebert (on Precept Austin) says the name has caused confusion with Luke 9:10, and identifies the feeding site as Bethsaida-Julias, east of the Jordan. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary)

**v. 48:**
- **How Jesus saw them.** Gill says Jesus saw them either with His eyes from the mountain or by His divine knowledge. The word for "straining" means tormented. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-48.htm)
- **The time.** Vincent and Guzik place the fourth watch at about 3–6 a.m. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-48.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/)
- **"He intended to pass by them."** Commentators read this in several ways:
  - **He only seemed to pass by.** Gill and JFB compare Luke 24:28, where Jesus acted as if He would go on. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-48.htm)
  - **He did it to prompt them.** Matthew Henry says Jesus did it to stir them to call out to Him, and that He would never really have passed them by. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-48.html)
  - **So they'd see the wind calm.** Another view on Bible Hub: so the disciples could clearly see the wind stilled when He came. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-48.htm)
  - **Guzik:** Jesus came over to them only after they cried out in fear. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/)

**v. 49–50:**
- The Pulpit Commentary says they thought He was a phantom partly because of the darkness. His seeming to pass by would have added to their fear. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-48.htm)
- *Contending for the Faith* notes that all twelve saw Him, so it wasn't one person's imagination. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-50.html)
- Sproul connects "It is I" with the Greek *ego eimi* ("I am"), a claim to be God. He rejects explanations about optical illusions or sandbars, because the Greek says Jesus walked on top of the water. (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-jesus-walking-water)

**v. 51–52:**
- **They should have known.** Matthew Henry says that if they had thought about the loaves, they wouldn't have been surprised. Multiplying bread showed as much power as walking on water. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_006.cfm)
- Constable says they had not yet learned that Jesus was God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-52.html)
- **Hardened hearts.** MacArthur says they "didn't connect the dots." (https://www.gty.org/sermons/41-31/jesus-walks-on-water) Sproul puts it down to hardened hearts that missed God in the flesh. (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-jesus-walking-water)

**v. 53:** The Bridgeway commentary says the boat was blown so far off course that they landed at Gennesaret, well west of where they were heading. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-50.html)

**v. 55:** Utley says the scene shows great need, chaos, and Jesus' compassion and power. Jesus always made time for people. (https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-6)

**v. 56:**
- **The fringe.** Ellicott says the "fringe" is better read as the hem or tassel. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-56.htm)
- **Why touch it.** JFB thinks people had heard about the woman healed in Mark 5. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-56.htm)
- **The power was in Christ.** A Bible Hub article says the healing power was in Christ's own authority, not the cloth. It adds that this was not grabbing at a "magic amulet." (https://biblehub.com/q/Significance_of_touching_Jesus_cloak.htm)
- **A blunter view.** Utley calls the crowd "desperate and superstitious and selfish." (https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-6)
- **Wider point.** Guzik says vv. 35–56 together show Jesus' power over the laws of nature. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/)

## Part 2: Where interpreters differ

I found no Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan or Anglican sources on this passage, and no clearly denominational disagreement. What I did find are differences between individual teachers:

**v. 48 ("pass by"):**
- **The Exodus/glory reading.** Sam Storms (charismatic) says Jesus wasn't trying to slip by unnoticed. He meant to reveal Himself as the God who "passed by" Moses. (https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/-he-meant-to-pass-by-them-) A Desiring God message (Baptist) agrees: you miss the point if you miss the Exodus echo. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/intertexuality-and-the-glory-of-god)
- **Utley's alternatives.** He suggests a link to Job 9:8, 11, or the meaning "join them," as one modern translation (TEV) has it. (https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-6)
- **Coffman's sharper view** (StudyLight labels him Restoration Movement/Arminian). He says that if the disciples had stayed hardened and not cried out, they could have lost their apostleship, and Jesus would have started again with other men. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-48.html) This contrasts with Henry and Gill (Gill labeled Calvinist), who say Jesus only seemed to pass by and never meant to. (Same page; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-48.htm)

**v. 52 (cause of the hardening):** Coffman links it to the disciples' dashed hopes of an earthly kingdom. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-48.html) The others simply say they had failed to understand Jesus' divine power.

## Part 3: Other views

**Catholic (v. 41):**
- Catholic Answers says the wording (took, blessed, broke, gave) is the language of the Eucharist, and that these loaves point forward to it. (https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/ministers-of-the-miracles)
- It quotes the Catechism (CCC 1335): the multiplied loaves "prefigure the superabundance of this unique bread of his Eucharist." (https://www.catholic.com/qa/was-jesus-feeding-of-the-5000-really-a-miracle-of-sharing)

**The "miracle of sharing" theory (vv. 41–44):** This view says the crowd simply shared food they had brought. Catholic Answers rejects it and says the bread was supernaturally produced. (https://www.catholic.com/qa/was-jesus-feeding-of-the-5000-really-a-miracle-of-sharing) The Precept Austin Matthew 14 page also rejects explaining the miracle away as an appeal to generosity. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary)

**Not found:** Orthodox (oca.org) readings, NET Bible notes beyond the v. 44 note quoted on Precept Austin, Bible Odyssey articles, and any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage.
